title: Safe and idempotent methods
summary: A method is safe if it does not modify the server state (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS).

sections.definition: A method is safe if it does not modify the server state (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS). It is idempotent if sending it once or ten times leaves the server in the same state (the safe ones, plus PUT and DELETE). POST and PATCH guarantee neither.
sections.analogy: The elevator button is idempotent: pressing it five times does not call five elevators. A coin-operated candy dispenser is not: each coin gets you another candy. Looking at the floor display is safe: it changes nothing.
sections.problem: It is the basis of retries. HTTP clients, load balancers and queues retry automatically when there are timeouts. If the method is idempotent, retrying does no harm; if it is not (POST), the retry can duplicate orders or charges, and it has to be protected with idempotency keys (see Idempotency in practice: keys and duplicate payments).
sections.code:wire:
# La red se cae justo después de enviar. ¿Reintento?
DELETE /v1/pedidos/1093   → 204    reintento → 404 o 204   estado final: borrado   ✔ seguro reintentar
PUT /v1/clientes/7 {...}  → 200    reintento → 200        estado final: igual     ✔ seguro reintentar
POST /v1/pagos {"monto":76000}  → 201 (id 501)
     reintento → 201 (id 502)     ✘ ¡dos cobros!
sections.code:server:
# Idempotencia se refiere al EFECTO en el servidor, no a la respuesta.
@app.delete("/v1/pedidos/{id}", status_code=204)
def borrar(id: int):
    pedidos.pop(id, None)   # si ya no existe, el estado final es el mismo
    # Algunos equipos devuelven 404 la segunda vez; sigue siendo idempotente.
sections.bad:
GET /v1/carrito/agregar?producto=42   ← GET con efecto: el prefetch del navegador lo dispara
PUT /v1/cuentas/7/saldo  {"sumar": 5000}  ← PUT no idempotente: cada reintento suma
sections.good:
POST /v1/carrito/items  {"producto_id":42}
PUT  /v1/cuentas/7/saldo  {"saldo": 125000}   ← valor absoluto: idempotente
sections.bridge:typescript: A retry loop in your own function that wraps fetch, applied to everything, is dangerous precisely because of this: retrying a GET is fine, but retrying a payment POST can charge twice. A well-built function that wraps fetch only retries idempotent methods or requests with an idempotency key.
sections.interview: A safe method is read-only: it must not change the server state, like GET, HEAD and OPTIONS. Idempotent means the effect of N identical requests is the same as that of one; all safe methods are, plus PUT and DELETE. POST is not and PATCH is not guaranteed. It matters because distributed systems have timeouts and automatic retries: retrying an idempotent method is harmless, but retrying a POST can duplicate an order or a payment, which is why idempotency keys are used for those operations.
sections.myths:
• Believing idempotent means "always returns the same response". A DELETE can respond 204 and then 404; what does not change is the state.
  • Thinking GET is safe because the framework guarantees it. It is a promise you keep or break in your code.
  • Assuming PATCH is never idempotent. It can be (set email = x), but the standard does not guarantee it (add 1 to the stock).

items.q: Which of these operations is idempotent?
items.why: Deleting order 9 twice leaves the same state: the order does not exist.

items.q: A GET /v1/reportes/generar creates a new file every time it is called. Which principle does it break?
items.why: GET must be safe. If it generates a file every time, it also stops being idempotent. It should be POST /v1/reportes.
It creates a resource and is not idempotent.
